newsitem.title: UK: British bank on trail of "smuggled" Nazi painting.
newsitem.headline: British bank on trail of "smuggled" Nazi painting.

text.p: A leading British bank, National Westminster, said on Friday it was checking its records to see if a Nazi agent deposited a valuable 16th century painting in one of its branches more than 50 years ago.
"We are looking into it but it is going to be difficult since we have over 2,700 branches," a NatWest spokeswoman said.
"It was such a long time ago and we may not have documents that show we ever held the painting."

According to a British Ministry of Economic Warfare letter sent to Britain's embassy in Lisbon in December 1944, a painting of "Salome" by the Italian artist Titian was smuggled from Portugal into Britain by a Nazi agent, Margarethe Duarte.

The document, which was among declassified U.S. intelligence reports recently obtained by a Jewish organisation in New York, said the painting was deposited in "a provincial branch of the Westminster Bank" in Duarte's name.

"It is also possible that the painting could have been deposited in someone else's name," the spokeswoman said, adding that even if a record is found, the bank may not be able to make the information public.
"We are legally bound to keep client information confidential," she said.
The Jewish Chronicle newspaper reported on Thursday the documents also showed Adolf Hitler had secret Swiss bank accounts into which he paid the royalties for his book "Mein Kampf".
The whereabouts of the painting is unknown. The British Ministry of Economic Warfare, which was set up in 1943 to disrupt Nazi Germany's economy, was disbanded after the war.

It is not known whether they ever traced the branch where the Titian was deposited but the answer could be hidden away in one of the 1,338 Ministry files being held at Britain's public records office, some of which are still classified.
The painting, it it exists, could be worth millions of dollars. But art experts warn that even if the painting is traced, it may not be authentic.
"The problem is that this could be a copy that was attributed to Titian," Rachel Mauro, art historian at fine art auctioneers Christies, told Reuters.
Mauro said art history scholarship during the 1940's was not as sophisticated as today and that many copies of Titian's work were erroneously attributed to the 16th century Italian master.
"How much Titian actually painted himself is subject to controversy," Mauro said.
Two authentic but different versions of Titian's Salome are known to exist -- one is in Madrid's Prado Museum and the other at the Doria Pamphilij Gallery in Rome.
Both paintings have been in the hands of those galleries for many years prior to World War II, Mauro said.

Researchers from the World Jewish Congress in New York have only recently been able to look at Second World War documents in the U.S. National Archives -- as part of an effort to locate the assets of Holocaust victims.
